title: Clustering Corrections for Limited-Pooling Treatment Effect Bounds with Heterogeneous Propensities
banked_reason: D0.5 math and decision panels passed, but the cold referee capped the delivered package at subfield (paper_score_ceiling 6.5 < 7.4) below the field floor; no bounded faithful same-topic repair remains.

proof_attempt_summary: The run derived and independently audited sharp source-endpoint corrections, joint endpoint geometry, matching second- versus fourth-order regular-grid correction rates, an unrestricted-class order-one obstruction, finite-sample ATE coverage, and an ATT extension. The mathematics and citation audit passed D0.5, but the field claim collapsed because source sharpness is not observational interval sharpness, the vanishing rates require a known Lipschitz subclass, and the DP optimizes only a conservative Bernoulli-half certificate. A future re-raise would need frozen application inputs and assumption-aligned comparators demonstrating informative corrected intervals, rather than another same-topic algebraic refinement.
tldr: Treatment-blind clustering of distinct covariates distorts Lee--Weidner limited-pooling bounds when propensities vary within cells. The note derives sharp global bounded-Lipschitz endpoint corrections, their joint geometry, finite-sample coverage, and a conservative optimized interval-partition certificate. On a regular line, the best even-cell corrections have matching rates \(\Theta((L/n)^{1/2})\) at second order and \(\Theta((L/n)^{2/3})\) at fourth order. These vanishing rates require the bounded-Lipschitz subclass: the unrestricted Lee--Weidner primitive class has a box-support correction at least the clustered sample mass. Target-aligned application width comparisons remain open in \texttt{oeq:interval-value}.
gap: Lee--Weidner applies clustering but explicitly leaves its theoretical analysis open. A small cluster diameter alone cannot control their count weights under heterogeneous propensity.
fill: Characterize the source-specific correction and its order-dependent decay, prove the regular-line separation, give finite-sample coverage and a clearly conservative optimized partition certificate, and test resulting interval width.
